 The Weekly Wrap: Florida Cities and Counties Are Reeling From Major Tax Cuts
 Federal permitting reform bill advances, study finds data centers bring few jobs, and more.
 Roshan Abraham   November 13, 2026

 Welcome back to The Weekly Wrap , our Friday roundup of stories that explain the problems oppressing people in cities and elevate the solutions that bring us closer to economic, environmental, and social justice. If you enjoy this newsletter, share it with a friend or colleague and tell them to subscribe . 
 Florida Ballot Amendment Cuts Property Taxes, Collapsing Revenue 
 Florida towns and counties are adjusting to a new financial reality after voters approved Proposition 3, which cut property taxes on “homesteaded” properties, according to Florida Today .
 The tax cut could cut up to half of local governments’ total revenue and result in the loss of firefighters, libraries, and library staff as well the creation of new fees to make up that lost revenue, according to Florida Policy Institute . The non-partisan research institute’s president, Jeff Brandes, drew an apocalyptic portrait of the cuts for Florida Today, telling the publication that entire cities could dissolve or merge with other cities to survive.
 The amendment caps non-residential property taxes to 5% a year, making it difficult for legislators to make up the difference with other taxes. Brandes predicts the legislature will eventually have to implement a new tax to compensate for the cuts. 
 Major Federal Permitting Reform Bill Advances 
 A controversial bipartisan permitting reform and energy infrastructure bill was advanced by the Senate this week. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 would speed up the approval of energy projects, whether they are renewable or fossil fuel-powered or used to power data centers, by narrowing the scopes of environmental laws including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act, and by streamlining the review process if permits are challenged. 
 According to TIME , the legislative package “could lead to more data centers powered by gas and built on public lands.” According to Mother Jones , the bill would speed up environmental review and restrict the ability of local governments to deny water quality certifications. Transit advocates are split on the bill , which would make it easier to build highways as well as make needed upgrades like bridge repairs. 
 Mississippi Votes In State’s First Black Senator Since the 19th Century 
 Lawyer and jurist Scott Colom has won a United States Senate race in Mississippi, making him the first Black senator for the state since 1881 and the first Democratic senator for the state since 1982, per the BBC .
 Colom won by about 5,000 votes by emphasizing access to healthcare and saving rural hospitals, according to NPR . A former district attorney, he had been nominated for a federal judgeship in 2023 but it was blocked by Cindy Hyde-Smith , the same senator he bested this month.
 Brooklyn Apartment Building Collapse Claims 8 Lives 
 In Flatbush, Brooklyn, a catastrophic apartment building collapse has killed eight people, including two children, according to Gothamist . Another 18 people were injured, with rescuers ending their search through the building’s rubble on Thursday afternoon. 
 The three-storey building was next door to a construction site where developers began excavating five months ago ; the landlord of the building that collapsed was jailed in 2006 for conditions at a separate building .
 In a statement, the New York State Tenant Bloc said the tragedy “stresses the urgency of taking buildings out of the hands of bad landlords who are looking to make a quick profit at the expense of people’s safety.” A City Reporter story following the collapse exposed problems with the city’s approach to doing just this: Several buildings transferred to landlord Mark Schwartz in September, despite an internal HPD document alleging that he had a business model that depended on skimping on repairs.
 Study Finds Data Centers Bring Few Lasting Jobs 
 A new peer-reviewed study published in the Journal of Regional Analysis & Policy found “negligible long-term increases in labor demand” from data center development in Texas from 2000 to 2024. 
 Analyzing 254 counties from 2000 to 2024, researchers found only a short-term boost in construction employment lasting roughly one to two years, and no statistically significant employment growth in information or professional and technical services, the high-tech sectors data centers are often expected to anchor. 
 In Abilene’s Taylor County, where data center development has expanded fastest, the sectors most tied to data centers added about 320 jobs, less than 5% of the roughly 6,700 jobs the county added overall. The authors say the findings suggest Texas’ data center tax incentives, which the state comptroller projects will cost $9 billion between 2025 and 2030, are an “inefficient” way to create local jobs.

 Roshan Abraham is a contributing editor for housing and homelessness at Next City. Based in Queens, New York, he has written extensively about city policy, including prisons and policing, housing and homelessness for The Guardian, The New York Times, Slate, The Baffler, Village Voice, The Verge, Pacific Standard, The Appeal, Vice and other outlets. At Vice, he was formerly a staff writer covering the housing beat. He is a former Open City Fellow and Witness Fellow at the Asian American Writers Workshop and a former Equitable Cities Fellow at Next City.
